# Summary {.unnumbered}

The EOD 2023 records each person's trips for one weekday as a chain. Reading the survey's
technical report and the tables together settles three things. The row order is the
sequence the person actually travelled — `folio_viaje` is only a generated number for it,
but the zones and the times pin the sequence down and the row order matches it — and the
reported start times are the noisy field, not the sequence. The
`{python} fmt(n_untimed)` trips with no start time are real trips whose questionnaire
block was lost, and the row after them is either the trip's own return or a duplicate of
it. And the survey's own answers contradict each other in a few hundred rows in ways the
tables let us arbitrate.

`eodgdl.load_eod()` reads the travel minutes a review corrected in place of the reported ones
(`{python} counts["leg_minutes_corrected"]` trips, @sec-minutes), applies its rules in five stages
before returning the trip table (@sec-fixes) and drops one kind of row only. It imputes the `{python} fmt(n_untimed)` untimed trips — `{python} counts["times_from_duplicate"]`
from the home-to-home row that duplicates them, which is then dropped, `{python} counts["times_from_neighbours"]`
from their nearest timed trips. It recodes the motives the chain contradicts —
`{python} counts["recoded_returns"] + counts["returns_elsewhere"]` "return home" trips that went elsewhere,
`{python} counts["arrivals_home"]` activity trips that arrived home, `{python} counts["daycare_escorts"]`
daycare escorts, `{python} counts["short_returns_other"]` returns nothing reads, to *Otros* — and sends home
`{python} counts["returns_copying_origin"] + counts["short_returns_home"]` returns recorded ending where they
started or somewhere nothing else touches. It keeps the `{python} counts["home_to_home"]` returns home made while already at home and the
`{python} counts["next_morning_returns"]` next-morning returns that close a night-shift day, but marks them as
non-trips; makes every trip start where the previous one ended and
`{python} fmt(counts["first_origins_copied"] + counts["first_origins_answered"] + counts["first_origins_typed"])` first
trips recorded leaving another zone start at home, and `{python} counts["first_trips_rotated"]` recorded from a
place to home go from home to the place; repairs `{python} fmt(counts["start_times_edited"])` mistyped
start hours in `{python} fmt(counts["chains_repaired"])` chains, reading a day past midnight only where it holds
together after it; and moves
`{python} counts["starts_at_arrival"]` starts that overlap the previous arrival to that arrival. Most of these
rules were the first hand pass's templates, turned into rules in the fourth review of the chains
(2026-09-26), and two of the next round's criteria became rules in the fifth, the same day. Every change is written to
the row in a new `ajustes` column and every defect left in a `problemas` column
(@tbl-flags), the residual defects of @sec-lingering included, so a consumer can keep, filter or weight the
`{python} fmt(n_rows_fixed)` rows that were changed and the `{python} fmt(n_rows_left)`
that still carry a defect. The model contract states chain order, the validator enforces what
a builder can guarantee, the builder leaves out the `{python} n_non_trips` marked non-trips,
and `tasha.chain_report` counts what remains. The chains the rules still leave inconsistent are
read by one scripted review round (@sec-revised).

What remains (@sec-lingering) is small and concentrated: `{python} pct(buildable_share)` of
person-days are monotone, continuous and home-to-home as they stand, and the defects in the
rest cluster in evening returns from work and in days that start or end away from home.
For an activity scheduler (@sec-scheduler) the residual errors cost a few percent of
episodes, filtered by rule; the instrument's own design — out-and-back tours, one weekday,
start times only, ages 6+ — bounds what the scheduler can learn far more than the errors do.

::: {.callout-note title="How to read the examples"}
Every example table shows a person's trips **as shipped**, with origin and destination
zones replaced by *home* when they equal the household's AGEB, and a final column
saying what `load_eod()` did to that row: `kept`, or the new start time, motive or origin
with the row's `ajustes` codes in brackets, and `left:` with the row's `problemas` codes
where a defect remains. All counts are recomputed when this document renders and the
structural claims are asserted, so a rendering failure is a real finding.
:::

# How the survey records trips {#sec-design}

The person questionnaire asks *¿Salió de su casa ayer?* and then *¿Cuántos viajes realizó
el día de ayer o el día hábil más reciente? (incluyendo ida y vuelta)* (Informe Técnico,
pp. 24–25). Each trip then gets a start hour and minute, a motive, a destination type, an
origin and destination zone, a main mode, and up to five legs. The origin *type* is asked
once, for the first trip, and repeated on every row.

| what | before fixes (as shipped) | after fixes (`load_eod()`) |
|---|---|---|
| dwellings / persons / trips / legs | `{python} fmt(n_viv)` / `{python} fmt(n_hab)` / `{python} fmt(n_trips)` / `{python} fmt(n_legs)` | `{python} fmt(n_viv)` / `{python} fmt(n_hab_c)` / `{python} fmt(n_trips_c)` / `{python} fmt(n_legs_c)` |
| persons who left home the day before | `{python} fmt(n_hab - said_no)` (`{python} pct((n_hab - said_no) / n_hab)`) | `{python} fmt(n_hab_c - said_no_c)` (`{python} pct((n_hab_c - said_no_c) / n_hab_c)`) |
| persons with at least one trip row that is a trip | `{python} fmt(travellers)` | `{python} fmt(travellers_c)` |
| said they left home but have no trip and no reason | `{python} fmt(said_yes_no_trips)` | `{python} fmt(said_yes_no_trips_c)` |
| `viajes_contados` equals the person's trip rows | always | always (one less for the `{python} n_dropped` persons whose duplicate left) |
| rows kept but marked as non-trips (`problemas`) | — | `{python} fmt(n_non_trips)` |
| rows dropped: home-to-home duplicates of an imputed return | — | `{python} n_dropped` |
| first trips that leave from *Su casa* | `{python} pct(first_from_home)` | `{python} pct(first_from_home_c)` |
| last trips that are *Regresar a Casa* | `{python} pct(last_is_return)` | `{python} pct(last_is_return_c)` |
| people whose day is a pure sequence of out-and-back pairs | `{python} pct(pure_share)` | `{python} pct(pure_share_c)` |
| maximum trips per person | `{python} max_trips` | `{python} max_trips_c` |

: The survey's trip section in numbers, before and after `load_eod`'s chain cleaning (@sec-fixes). Only the `{python} n_dropped` duplicate returns leave the tables; the `{python} n_zero_recoded` people whose only rows are returns made from home keep them, marked, and count as travellers no longer. The "after" pattern and anchor figures are over the chain without the marked non-trips. {#tbl-design}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-trips-per-person
#| tbl-cap: "Trips per traveller. The instrument elicits tours: even counts dominate, and a person with exactly two trips is the modal day."
tc = trip_count_tbl.rename("travellers").reset_index().rename(columns={"index": "trips"})
tc.columns = ["trips", "travellers"]
tc["share"] = (tc.travellers / travellers).map(lambda x: pct(x))
show(tc)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-patterns
#| tbl-cap: "The eight most common day patterns, one letter per trip: A an activity, H a return home, ? a trip with no motive (the untimed rows of @sec-untimed). The cumulative share runs down the table."
pt = seq_tbl.rename("people").reset_index().rename(columns={"motivo_viaje": "pattern", "index": "pattern"})
pt.columns = ["pattern", "people"]
pt["share of travellers"] = (pt.people / travellers).map(pct)
pt["cumulative share"] = (pt.people.cumsum() / travellers).map(pct)
show(pt)
```

Two design facts matter downstream. The day is a **weekday**: the weekday question allows
only Monday to Friday, and weekend travel is captured only as person-level checkboxes on
modes and destinations, never as trips. And the reference day is looser than "yesterday":
the reported weekday is the working day before the interview date for
**`{python} pct(ref_match)`** of persons, `{python} fmt(same_day)` name the interview
weekday itself, and members of `{python} fmt(hh_disagree)` of the `{python} fmt(hh_with_day)`
households with a travel day do not agree on it. Treat it as *a recent weekday*.

# Which order is the chain {#sec-order}

The model contract used to say trips are numbered "in start-time order". The builder had
always used the row order, `folio_viaje`. The two disagree for
**`{python} fmt(n_dis)`** people: `{python} fmt(n_inv_raw)` trips start earlier than the
trip before them, and only `{python} overnight_raw` of those look like an overnight wrap.

Zone continuity — does each trip start where the previous one ended — is the test that
does not depend on the times, and it is decisive (@tbl-order). Sorting by start time
destroys chains that row order keeps intact, and it would make *Regresar a Casa* the first
trip of `{python} fmt(time_first_return)` of the `{python} fmt(n_dis)` people. The row
order is the sequence; the times are wrong where they disagree.

`folio_viaje` itself is a generated sequence number and carries no information of its own,
so the question is whether the data pin the sequence without it. They do (@tbl-perm). For
clean days with three or more trips, the row order is the *only* permutation that is both
zone-continuous and time-monotone in `{python} pct(unique_share)` of cases. Where the row
order has a defect, no permutation does better: of the `{python} n_brk_people` people with
a zone break, `{python} n_cont_none` admit no continuous ordering at all and only
`{python} n_cont_timed` of the rest has one the times agree with, so the breaks are wrong
zones, not wrong sequence (@sec-origin). Re-sequencing whole home-based tours by time, with
the home anchors kept, resolves `{python} reseq_removed` of the `{python} fmt(inv_total)`
inversions for `{python} n_reseq` people — `{python} reseq_within` of them days spent
entirely inside the home zone, where the tour boundaries are guesses, and
`{python} reseq_overnight` overnight-looking days where the night-shift reading is the
natural one (household 299, person 1: work at 22:00, home at 06:00, which re-sequencing
turns into a return before a night shift). It was not adopted.

| test | result |
|---|---|
| clean days with 3+ trips where the row order is the only continuous, monotone permutation | `{python} pct(unique_share)` of `{python} fmt(n_clean_multi)` |
| people with a zone break: no continuous ordering exists | `{python} n_cont_none` of `{python} n_brk_people` |
| people with a zone break: a continuous ordering the times agree with | `{python} n_cont_timed` |
| tour re-sequencing: inversions removed | `{python} reseq_removed` of `{python} fmt(inv_total)` |
| tour re-sequencing: people affected, within-zone days, overnight-looking days | `{python} n_reseq`, `{python} reseq_within`, `{python} reseq_overnight` |

: What a permutation search over each person's trips finds, on the table with the untimed trips of @sec-untimed imputed. {#tbl-perm}

| | row order (`folio_viaje`) | start-time order |
|---|---|---|
| continuity, all adjacent pairs | `{python} pct(cont_raw, 2)` (`{python} fmt(breaks_raw)` breaks) | — |
| continuity, the `{python} fmt(n_dis)` people with non-monotone times | `{python} pct(cont_folio_dis)` (`{python} brk_folio_dis` breaks) | `{python} pct(cont_time_dis)` (`{python} fmt(brk_time_dis)` breaks) |
| those people whose first trip would be a return home | `{python} folio_first_return` | `{python} fmt(time_first_return)` |

: Zone continuity under the two candidate orders. {#tbl-order}

Of the `{python} fmt(n_inv_raw)` out-of-order trips, `{python} pct(inv_return_share, 0)` are
*Regresar a Casa* and `{python} pct(inv_after_work, 0)` follow a *Trabajar*: the evening
return from work is where the times go wrong.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-order
#| tbl-cap: "A chain whose times are out of order but whose zones chain perfectly in row order (household 87, person 3). Trip 4 is a 9:40 that can only be 21:40; the repair of @sec-clock reads it so."
show(person_table((87, 3)))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-order2
#| tbl-cap: "The same defect where no single-trip rule helps (household 8, person 3): a work trip at 19:00 followed by returns and departures whose times contradict each other while the zones chain. The search of @sec-clock reads the 19:00 as 09:00, an extra leading 1, and the closing 18:00 as 20:00: with a 30-minute drive the two-minute step at the end is a 32-minute contradiction."
show(person_table((8, 3)))
```

# Problems found and fixed {#sec-fixes}

`load_eod()` reads the travel minutes a review corrected first (@sec-minutes), then applies the
rules below in five stages — what the questionnaire lost (@sec-untimed), motives and destinations
(@sec-mislabel to @sec-daycare), the rows that are not trips and where the other returns went
(@sec-home, @sec-elsewhere, @sec-nightshift), where the trips start and end (@sec-origin to
@sec-short) and start times (@sec-clock to @sec-night) — and
`load_eod(clean_chains=False)` returns the survey as shipped. One kind of row is dropped, the `{python} n_dropped`
home-to-home returns that duplicate an imputed return (@sec-untimed); the trip table keeps
its other `{python} fmt(n_trips_c)` rows, and two columns record what happened to each. `ajustes` names
every change the rules made to the row and `problemas` every defect they left, as
semicolon-joined codes (@tbl-flags); `eodgdl.chains.has_code` filters on one, and
`eodgdl.chains.non_trips` picks out the rows marked as not being trips, which the model build
leaves out. Each rule's evidence is also the docstring of its function in `eodgdl.chains`.
@tbl-errors lists every kind of error this note found, how many trips carried it as
shipped, and how many still do after the rules; the shares are of the
`{python} fmt(n_trips)` trips as shipped and of the `{python} fmt(len(C))` in the chain
`load_eod()` returns once the `{python} n_non_trips` non-trips are set aside. Every error
left is a code on its row: the last row of @tbl-errors, the trips carrying at least one
error, is the number of chain trips with a non-empty `problemas`
(`{python} fmt(any_C)`), and the `{python} fmt(n_rows_left)` rows with one in the full
table add the `{python} n_non_trips` marked non-trips. A row carries at most one of the
five time-order codes (`chains.TIME_ORDER_ISSUES`): `hora_invertida` is the contradiction
beyond the tolerance, the other four are what it does not cover — after the rules only
`hora_nocturna` among them, the rest moved to the arrival (@sec-arrival); `hora_2301` and
`hora_madrugada` mark the reported value itself and may sit beside one of them.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-flags
#| tbl-cap: "The vocabulary of the two columns load_eod adds to the trip table, with the number of trips carrying each code. A row can carry several, joined by ';'."
show(flag_vocab)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-errors
#| tbl-cap: "Every kind of trip error found, before and after the rules; the after column is over the chain without the marked non-trips. The treatment column says what the rules do to each; what they leave is for the review or the consumer, each under a `problemas` code named there, and @tbl-lingering gives them as person-days. Errors overlap, so the last row counts trips carrying at least one of them rather than the sum of the column; after the rules it equals the chain trips with a non-empty `problemas`."
#| output: asis
print(md_table(error_rows,
               ["error", "trips as shipped", "share", "trips after `load_eod()`", "share", "treatment"]))
```

## The travel minutes a review corrected come first {#sec-minutes}

Every rule that reads a start time reads it against the previous trip's arrival, its start plus
its leg minutes, so the minutes are part of what the rules read. A motorised trip that reports
twice the survey's typical minutes for its mode over its straight-line distance — the median of
the survey's trips of that mode in that distance band, AGEB centroid to centroid — reports the
error, not the clock: the ninth hand round gave `{python} n_minutes_trips` such trips
(`{python} n_minutes_legs` legs) the typical minutes, and the person's other trips over the same
route the same. Until the fifth review of the chains (2026-09-26) those were hand decisions applied
after the rules, so the typo search read the reported minutes and the hand undid its readings start
by start; since then they are a table, `eodgdl/revisions/leg_minutes.csv.gz`, that `load_eod`
reads before any rule, spreading a trip's minutes over its legs in proportion (`minutos:revision`).
Household 7425, person 3 (@tbl-ex-minutes) reports 120 minutes for each of four trips to work and
back: the afternoon shift at 14:10 starts before the ride home from the morning one could have ended,
and the search read the last two starts two hours later. With 60 minutes the survey's own hours hold.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-minutes
#| tbl-cap: "Minutes that were the error (household 7425, person 3): 120 minutes for a 60-minute ride. Read before the rules, the survey's hours stand."
show(person_table(ex_minutes))
```

## Untimed trips are lost questionnaires, and are imputed {#sec-untimed}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-nulls
#| tbl-cap: "Missing values on the trip rows as shipped, for the fields a chain needs. The untimed rows lack exactly the questionnaire block — time, motive, destination type — and nothing else."
nt = null_tbl.rename("missing").reset_index().rename(columns={"index": "field"})
nt.columns = ["field", "missing"]
show(nt)
```

`{python} fmt(n_untimed)` trips report neither hour nor minute. They also lack the motive
and the destination type, but every one of them carries origin and destination zones, a
mode, legs with minutes and a duration band: they are real trips whose questionnaire block
was not captured. `{python} pct(april_share, 0)` were interviewed in April 2023, the last
month of fieldwork. None is a person's last trip; `{python} pos_first` are first trips
and the rest sit mid-chain.

The row after an untimed block is a *Regresar a Casa* in almost every case, at 18:00–20:59
`{python} pct(after_evening, 0)` of the time, with the block's mode (@tbl-blocks). After
a single untimed trip it is that trip's own return, so the block is a lost outbound
questionnaire (@tbl-ex-single). After a multi-trip block that already ended at home it goes
from home to home, with the block's last mode and duration: a duplicate of the block's
return carrying the answers (@tbl-ex-multi).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-blocks
#| tbl-cap: "The untimed blocks by size and whether they end in the home zone, with what the next row looks like. A single untimed trip is followed by its own return; a multi-trip block ending at home is followed by a home-to-home duplicate."
bt = block_tbl.rename(columns={"k": "untimed trips in block", "next_return": "next row is a return",
                               "next_home_to_home": "next row goes home→home", "same_mode": "same mode as block"})
bt["same mode as block"] = bt["same mode as block"].map(pct)
show(bt)
```

The person in @tbl-ex-single is `{python} label(ex_single)`.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-single
#| tbl-cap: "A single untimed trip: trip 3 lost its questionnaire block, trip 4 is its return. Trip 3 takes the motive its nearest timed trips vote for and a start counted back from trip 4."
show(person_table(ex_single))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-multi
#| tbl-cap: "A multi-trip block (household 889, person 1): trips 3–4 are an out-and-back by bus with no answers, and trip 5 repeats trip 4 from home to home with a time and a motive attached. Trip 4 takes trip 5's answers, trip 5 is dropped as the duplicate, and trip 3 is imputed from its neighbours."
show(person_table(ex_multi))
```

**The fix.** Until 2026-09-03 `load_eod()` excluded the whole person from `hab` and
`trips`, on the grounds that a day with an unobservable trip cannot support activity
scheduling; an earlier rule had dropped only the untimed rows, which kept the duplicates and
stitched chains across the hole. Both threw away real trips: the
`{python} len(untimed_persons)` persons are `{python} pct(len(untimed_persons) / n_hab, 2)`
of the sample and `{python} pct(untimed_w_share, 2)` of weighted trips, they average
`{python} f"{untimed_trips_per_person:.1f}"` trips against
`{python} f"{all_trips_per_person:.1f}"` overall, so the exclusion leaned on complex days,
and keeping them with zero trips would have lifted the no-travel share from
`{python} pct(notravel_now, 2)` to `{python} pct(notravel_if_excluded, 2)`. `load_eod()`
now keeps the person and fills the lost block in two steps.

*The duplicates first.* A motive-less row that comes from elsewhere into the home zone is a
return home, and when the row after it is a timed *Regresar a Casa* from home to home, that
row is the return's own questionnaire block attached to a duplicate. The return takes its
motive and, where it had none, its time (`motivo:duplicado`, `hora:duplicado`), and the
duplicate is dropped once every rule has run, the only rows `load_eod()` removes, since its
answers now sit on the return and the person was already home (`viajes_contados` is reduced
by one for those persons): `{python} counts["duplicate_returns"]` pairs, the
last row of every multi-trip block that ends at home (@tbl-ex-multi) plus one timed trip
with no motive.

*The rest by their nearest neighbours.* Every other row without a motive —
`{python} counts["motives_from_neighbours"]`, of which `{python} counts["times_from_neighbours"]`
also lack a time and `{python} n_timed_no_motive` are timed — takes the vote of its 30
nearest timed activity trips whose own times hold up. The imputation runs before the typo
search of @sec-clock, so a mistyped hour on a donor would enter the vote as shipped: of the
`{python} fmt(n_candidates)` timed activity trips with a timed successor,
`{python} fmt(n_neg_duration)` have a negative activity duration — the next trip starts
before this one could have arrived, by a median of `{python} fmt(neg_duration_median)`
minutes, the 12-hour-clock and leading-1 entries — and `{python} n_early_start` start before
their own predecessor could have arrived beyond the tolerance; neither may donate
(`_donor_mask`), which leaves `{python} fmt(n_donors)`. Distance is a weighted count of mismatches over the main
mode, the sex and occupation of the traveller, the person's own earlier motive at the same
destination zone, whether the trip stays in one zone, leaves from home, is followed by a
return home, is the first of the day, or follows a work or school trip, plus the scaled
differences in leg minutes, the next trip's start hour and age
(`eodgdl.chains._IMPUTE_WEIGHTS`). The most common motive among the thirty is written, with the
most common destination type among the donors that voted for it (`motivo:vecinos`). The
start time is then counted back from the next trip: its start, less this trip's leg minutes,
less the median activity duration of those donors, kept between the previous trip's arrival
and the next trip's start (`hora:vecinos`). Blocks are filled back to front, so every row
has a timed successor when its turn comes. Returns home never come out of the vote, since
the donors are activity trips; every untimed row is an activity or a duplicated return, so
none needs one.

**How well it works.** The matcher can be scored on trips whose answers are known.
@tbl-score takes `{python} fmt(len(samp))` timed trips of the same shape as the untimed ones
— from home, followed by a return, not the first of the day, on foot, by car or by bus,
with the return between 17:00 and 22:00 — hides each person's own trips from the donor
pool, and compares the vote with the answer. The motive is right about twice as often as
the most common motive would be, and almost always where the person had already visited
the zone that day; the start lands a median of `{python} fmt(err_median)` minutes from the
true one, where the midpoint of the window between the neighbouring trips — what the
rejected 2026-09-01 prototype used — lands `{python} fmt(mid_median)` away. The vote
over-produces the most common answer: `{python} pct(pred_share.iloc[0], 0)` of its answers
are *`{python} pred_share.index[0]`* against `{python} pct(true_share.get(pred_share.index[0], 0), 0)`
in truth, so the imputed motives are plausible one by one and skewed as a set.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-score
#| tbl-cap: "The matcher scored on timed trips of the untimed trips' shape, with the person's own trips withheld from the donor pool."
show(score_tbl)
```

**Effect.** `{python} fmt(n_untimed)` trips gain a start time and
`{python} counts["motives_from_duplicate"] + counts["motives_from_neighbours"]` a motive and
a destination type; they are `{python} pct(imp_w_share, 2)` of weighted trips. Of the
`{python} counts["motives_from_neighbours"]` motives the neighbours supplied,
`{python} int(imputed_motives.iloc[0])` are *`{python} imputed_motives.index[0]`* and
`{python} int(imputed_motives.iloc[1])` *`{python} imputed_motives.index[1]`* (@tbl-imputed);
`{python} pct(imputed_evening, 0)` of the imputed start times fall between 17:00 and 19:59,
just before the evening returns that follow them. The neighbouring times are read as
shipped, so a mistyped neighbour gives a mistyped imputation, which the search of
@sec-clock never edits: `{python} imputed_left` imputed rows end up marked
`hora_invertida`. Every imputed row carries its codes in `ajustes`, so an estimation that
wants only observed answers can drop them.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-imputed
#| tbl-cap: "The motives the nearest-neighbour vote wrote on the rows that had none."
im = imputed_motives.rename("trips").reset_index(); im.columns = ["motive", "trips"]
show(im)
```

## A return home made while already at home is not a trip {#sec-home}

In the shipped table, `{python} first_return_from_home` first trips are *Regresar a Casa*
leaving from *Su casa*, and `{python} consecutive_returns` trips are a *Regresar a Casa*
immediately after another. Walking each chain with an at-home flag — set when the first trip
leaves from *Su casa* in the household's zone, then from each kept trip's motive — flags
`{python} counts["home_to_home"]` rows after the imputation of @sec-untimed and the motive
rules (`{python} hh_first` first trips, `{python} len(hh_rows) - hh_first` later ones).
`{python} hh_home_zone` of them start and end in the home zone and `{python} hh_last` are the
person's last trip. Many are the return recorded twice: an activity trip that arrived home,
now read as the return (@sec-arrivals), and a *Regresar a Casa* from home to home with the same
mode and minutes after it. Elsewhere the leg minutes usually differ from the return they
follow, so a within-zone errand coded as "return home" is the likeliest reading, and in the
model such a row is unschedulable either way.

The first trip needs the zone as well as the type because the origin type is one answer per
person: the survey asks where the day started and repeats the answer on every row (no person
carries two origin types). `{python} first_return_from_away` of the first-trip returns answer
*Su casa* but leave another zone, so they were made away from home, and they are trips
(`{python} first_return_only_trip` of them the person's only trip). Until 2026-09-25 the answer
alone set the flag and these rows were marked too; since the fourth review of the chains the
answer of such a day names where it started (@sec-copied).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-hh1
#| tbl-cap: "A double return (household 5, person 1): trip 3 leaves home for home an hour after the person got there."
show(person_table((5, 1)))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-hh2
#| tbl-cap: "A day made only of returns (household 306, person 6): both rows leave from Su casa for the home zone. Both are kept and marked; the build sees no trips for this person, who counts as a non-traveller (@sec-zero)."
show(person_table((306, 6)))
```

**Effect.** `{python} counts["home_to_home"]` rows are kept and marked `regreso_en_casa`: the
`{python} n_non_trips` rows `eodgdl.chains.non_trips` picks out and the builder leaves out, the
`{python} counts["duplicate_returns"]` duplicates of @sec-untimed having been dropped, and the
`{python} counts["next_morning_returns"]` next-morning returns of @sec-nightshift marked beside them. No
trip in the built table goes from H to H (the contract forbids it, and `validate` checks).

## A "return home" that did not reach the home zone takes its destination type {#sec-mislabel}

`{python} n_mis` *Regresar a Casa* trips carry a destination type other than *Su casa*.
The destination zone arbitrates: `{python} mis_home` of them land in the household's zone,
so the motive is corroborated and the type is the stale answer — they keep their motive
(@tbl-ex-keep). The other `{python} int(mis_away.sum())` did not reach the home zone, so the
motive is wrong whatever the type says, and the type is the best label there is
(@tbl-recode). `{python} stale_type` of those repeat the previous trip's type and
`{python} went_nowhere` stay in its zone, so some labels are probably stale too; but each is
a trip that ended away from home, and any activity beats a return.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-recode
#| tbl-cap: "The 84 recoded returns: the destination type they reported and the motive load_eod now gives them (the table _MOTIVO_POR_TIPO_LUGAR_DESTINO in eodgdl.eod)."
show(recode_tbl)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-recode
#| tbl-cap: "Recoded (household 75, person 3): trip 2 says return home but lands in a third zone with type Otros; it becomes Otros, and the day is read as one that never went home."
show(person_table((75, 3)))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-keep
#| tbl-cap: "Kept (household 144, person 2): trip 2 says return home with type Fábrica o taller, copied from trip 1, but it lands in the home zone after a two-hour ride on the works bus. The zone corroborates the motive."
show(person_table((144, 2)))
```

**Effect.** `{python} counts["recoded_returns"]` motives change. Because a recoded trip
leaves the person away from home, `{python} rescued` rows that the home-to-home rule had
been dropping — recoded returns after another return, and the genuine returns home after
them — are kept, and the `{python} recoded_work`
recoded *Trabajar* trips now set an `EmploymentZone` like any other. `{python} mis_last`
of the recoded trips were the last of the day, which now ends away from home.

## A "return home" recorded ending where it started went home {#sec-copied-return}

A *Regresar a Casa* whose destination AGEB is its own origin's, away from the home zone, copied
its origin into its destination: the motive and the place type (*Su casa*) both say home, and
only the copied AGEB says otherwise — the mirror of the first trips recorded leaving their own
destination (@sec-copied). The recode of @sec-mislabel reads a return typed as a place first;
of the returns left, `{python} counts["returns_copying_origin"]` are so recorded, and `load_eod`
sets their destination to the home zone (`destino:copia`). The first hand pass had moved every
one of the 67 it reviewed home and read none as an activity there.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-copy-return
#| tbl-cap: "A return recorded ending in the AGEB it left: its destination becomes home."
show(person_table(ex_copy_return))
```

## An activity trip that arrives home is the return home {#sec-arrivals}

The zone and the place type can both say home while the motive says an activity: a trip that
arrives at *Su casa* in the household's zone from another zone, typed with the motive of the
place it came from. It is the mirror of the returns of @sec-mislabel, and such trips nearly
always follow an activity at their origin and precede a trip that leaves home.
`{python} counts["arrivals_home"]` trips after the day's first are so recorded, and `load_eod`
recodes them *Regresar a Casa* (`motivo:casa`); where the next row repeats the return from home
to home with the same mode and minutes, the walk of @sec-home then marks it a non-trip. The hand
passes had recoded 229 of the 270 such trips including first trips (the first pass 95, the
sixth 134) and kept most of the rest as first trips recorded from a place to home whose place
was really the day's first destination (the fifth pass's rotated records), which is why a
first trip is left to the review.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-arrival
#| tbl-cap: "An activity trip that arrives home from another zone: it is the return, and a home-to-home row after it repeats it."
show(person_table(ex_arrival))
```

## A daycare trip from age 12 is an escort {#sec-daycare}

The survey uses *Guardería* both for the child who attends daycare and for whoever takes the
child there or brings it back, and it interviews ages 6 and over, so a traveller of 12 or more
is the escort. `{python} counts["daycare_escorts"]` *Guardería* trips are made from that age, by
`{python} len(escort_people)` people, `{python} escort_adults` of them adults; `load_eod` recodes
them *Llevar o recoger a alguien* (`motivo:guarderia`), which the model reads as an escort (F),
and they no longer make their traveller a student. The hand passes had recoded every one (the
first pass 118, the ninth round 46) and put the children's back (the seventh pass, 23); the
model build reads the age the same way. The `{python} len(guard)` trips left are all children's
(@sec-lingering-purpose). The person in @tbl-ex-guarderia is `{python} label(ex_guarderia)`, aged
`{python} int(clean.hab.edad.loc[ex_guarderia])`.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-guarderia
#| tbl-cap: "An adult's Guardería trip: the escort of a child, recoded as such."
show(person_table(ex_guarderia))
```

## A "return home" that went elsewhere takes the motive of the place {#sec-elsewhere}

A *Regresar a Casa* that ends away from home, in another AGEB than the one it left, and that
neither its type (@sec-mislabel) nor a copied destination (@sec-copied-return) reads as reaching
home, went to a place — unless the person made it from home, in which case it is no trip at all
(@sec-home). What the person does there is what their own trips to that AGEB do: the most common
motive among them and its place type. Where no other trip goes there and the day started there,
it is what the day-start answer names. `{python} counts["returns_elsewhere"]` returns are read so
(`motivo:lugar`) and `{python} counts["short_returns_home"] + counts["short_returns_other"]` are left with nothing
to go by, which @sec-short reads once the origins are continuous. The first hand pass had recoded 87 such
returns, 56 of them to *Trabajar* — 20 of those for students, homemakers or children, a default
rather than a reading.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-elsewhere
#| tbl-cap: "A return home that ends at a place the person's own trips visit: it takes their motive there."
show(person_table(ex_elsewhere))
```

## The next morning's return of a night shift is not a trip of the day {#sec-nightshift}

A night worker's diary opens with the morning return from the job — the day starts at work,
and the person's answer names the workplace — and records the evening departure for it. When
the day's last row is a return home from that workplace, right after the trip to it that starts
at 18:00 or later, that row is the next morning's return: a repeat of the first one a day on,
its hour usually an evening one (19:00–20:59, the morning's typed on the wrong side of the
clock). The survey day ends at work. `{python} counts["next_morning_returns"]` days end so; the
row is kept and marked `regreso_dia_siguiente`, and the build leaves it out. Hand passes 2 and 3
had dropped the last row of every such day they reviewed (62), and the rule applies the
convention to all of them.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-night
#| tbl-cap: "A night shift: the day opens with the morning return from the job and ends with the evening trip to it; the last row, a return from the same place, is the next morning's."
show(person_table(ex_night))
```

## Mistyped start hours {#sec-clock}

The out-of-order times are not random noise: they are mistyped hours, and the typos have
a small vocabulary. An afternoon or evening hour entered on a 12-hour clock (5:30 for
17:30); an extra leading 1 (19:00 for 9:00); a missing one (8:00 for 18:00); and now and
then both on one field (18:00 for 20:00). Household 8, person 3 (@tbl-ex-order2) reads
coherently under exactly that vocabulary, and the reading generalises into a search. A
chain is feasible when every trip starts no earlier than the previous trip's arrival — its
start plus its leg minutes — less `{python} _START_TIME_TOLERANCE` minutes of tolerance for
rounding; an overnight wrap between a trip at or after 18:00 and one by 06:00 is a night
shift, not a violation, and so is a return home before 10:00 after a trip to work that left at
18:00 or later (below). For every infeasible chain the first menu of @tbl-edits is tried on each
trip and the cheapest combination that makes the chain feasible is kept. It is applied only
if it is unique, costs at most `{python} _START_TIME_MAX_COST` and leaves
`{python} _MIN_MANDATORY_STAY` minutes or more at work or school. Where the first menu finds no
reading, the second adds a morning start typed as an evening one (`hora:-12h`, from 17:00 on).
Three guards keep it honest: a wrap is accepted only between two unedited trips, so the search
cannot manufacture a night shift; the leading-1 and −12 h edits are allowed only where they yield
a morning hour, so they cannot invent trips before dawn; and a reading may not leave the person
at work or school for less than half an hour. A chain with no such reading is left as it is.

The second menu, the stay at work, the night window and the cost cap (4 until then) came in the
fourth review of the chains (2026-09-26), from the first hand pass's readings of the chains the
search had left: 550 of its 1,026 start edits read an evening start as the morning's
("Corrección AM/PM"), most on a day's first trip to work recorded at 20:00–22:59 and followed by
a return in the afternoon. Tried first, the −12 h entry changed 241 readings the first menu
already made, none for the better, so it is a second menu. The night window goes the other way:
a return home recorded between 06:01 and 09:59 after a departure for work at 18:00 or later is
the next morning's — 19:00 to 07:00 and 20:00 to 08:00 are the factories' shifts — but the
search read 34 such returns as the same evening's, a median 39 minutes after the arrival at
work, and the first pass read 56 more as day shifts by moving both hours by twelve. Now
`{python} int(night_shift_c.sum())` returns are read as the night shift they are. The stay at
work rules out readings such as household 15423, person 1's: to work at 07:30, 35 minutes, home
at 17:50 and to the shops at 18:00, where an extra leading 1 read off the 17:50 closed a
25-minute overlap by leaving no minutes at work.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-edits
#| tbl-cap: "The edit menus, one row per way a start hour can have been mistyped, with the cost the search minimises. The costs rank the mechanisms by how common they are and break ties between readings that would otherwise be equally cheap; the second menu is tried only where the first reads nothing."
show(menu)
```

Every edited row is marked in the `ajustes` column with the edit applied (`hora:+12h`,
`hora:-12h`, `hora:-10h`, `hora:+10h`, `hora:-10h+12h`), so a consumer can treat those start times as
uncertain — which they are: each is the most economical reading of a contradiction, not an
observation. An imputed start time (@sec-untimed) cannot carry a typo and is never edited.
A chain with no unique reading is left as it is, and the trips in it that still start before
the previous arrival are marked `hora_invertida` in `problemas`. The search replaced an earlier rule that added 12 hours to a single trip when
that alone restored the order. It moves `{python} strict_same` of that rule's
`{python} n_strict` rows identically, reads `{python} strict_contradicted` differently because
the arrival constraint rules out the 12-hour reading there, and leaves
`{python} strict_unmoved` in chains it cannot resolve as a whole.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-repair
#| tbl-cap: "What the search does on the table after the previous rules, and what it leaves."
show(pd.concat([repair_tbl, edits_tbl.rename(columns={"edit": "measure", "rows": "value"}).assign(measure=lambda d: "rows edited by " + d.measure, value=lambda d: d.value.map(fmt))]))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-clock
#| tbl-cap: "A 12-hour entry (household 31, person 2): work at 8:00, an errand at 6:00 that must be 18:00, home at 19:00."
show(person_table((31, 2)))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-missing1
#| tbl-cap: "A missing leading 1 (household 290, person 4): work at 11:00 and home at 8:00. Reading the return as 20:00 would overtake the 18:13 pick-up, so the search reads it as 18:00 instead."
show(person_table((290, 4)))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-compound
#| tbl-cap: "Both errors on one field (household 430, person 4): an evening class recorded at 18:05 and 19:36 after a return at 19:00. The cheapest monotone reading moves the class to 20:05 and 21:36; a night shift built from the earlier trips would be cheaper still, but a wrap between edited trips is not allowed."
show(person_table((430, 4)))
```

**Effect.** `{python} fmt(counts["start_times_edited"])` rows in
`{python} fmt(counts["chains_repaired"])` chains change; `{python} moved_after_evening` of
them follow a trip starting at or after 17:00 and could be genuine night-shift returns,
which is the search's known risk. No edited hour falls before 05:00. @fig-hours shows the
shift in the returns-home clock.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hours
#| fig-cap: "Returns home by start hour, as shipped and after cleaning, for the morning hours where the mistyped entries sat. The afternoon and evening hours gain what these lose."
#| fig-alt: "Grouped bar chart of the number of 'Regresar a Casa' trips by start hour from 0 to 12. Grey bars for the shipped survey stand above orange bars for the cleaned table in hours 1 to 6, most visibly at 1, 2 and 5 o'clock, and the two are nearly equal from 7 o'clock on."
hrs = np.arange(0, 13)
a = hour_raw.reindex(hrs).fillna(0); b = hour_clean.reindex(hrs).fillna(0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 3.8))
ax.bar(hrs - 0.2, a, 0.4, color=GREY, label="as shipped")
ax.bar(hrs + 0.2, b, 0.4, color=ORANGE, label="after load_eod")
ax.set_xticks(hrs); ax.set_xlabel("start hour of 'Regresar a Casa' trips"); ax.set_ylabel("trips")
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.legend(frameon=False)
for s in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## A day that starts in the small hours with a long stay is a mistyped hour {#sec-early}

The search reads a chain only where its times contradict each other, and a mistyped hour can
leave the order intact. `{python} n_early` days start between 01:00 and 04:59 with a trip to
school, shops, sport, a visit or the doctor, and a stay of eight hours or more follows
`{python} n_early_long` of them (median `{python} f"{early_long_median:.0f}"` hours). The
clearest are school days: `{python} len(school_1)` start at 01:xx and `{python} school_1_back`
of them come home between 18:00 and 20:59, as `{python} fmt(school_13_back)` of the
`{python} fmt(len(school_13))` school days that start at 13:xx do — the afternoon shift typed
on a 12-hour clock (@tbl-ex-early). No code marked them, since their order holds. Since
2026-09-26 the search also runs on a chain whose first trip, to anything but work, starts
before 05:00 with a stay of eight hours or more after it, and counts that start as
infeasible; the menu, the cost cap and the uniqueness rule are the same.
`{python} counts["early_starts_read"]` days are read this way. The short early trips — a
market at 04:30, an escort before dawn — keep their hours, and every day's first trip to
anything but work still before 05:00 is marked `hora_madrugada` (`{python} n_madrugada`
after the rules). Forcing every such start past 05:00 was tried and dropped: it read genuine
early market trips as afternoon ones.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-early
#| tbl-cap: "An afternoon school shift typed on a 12-hour clock: school at 01:xx, home in the evening. The search reads the departure 12 hours later."
show(person_table(ex_early))
```

## A start before the previous arrival, by minutes, moves to it {#sec-arrival}

A trip that leaves before the previous one could have arrived, by
`{python} _START_TIME_TOLERANCE` minutes or less, is not an hour typed wrong: the overlaps
spike at round leg minutes — `{python} pct(slide_round, 0)` of them are exactly 5, 10 or 15
minutes — the rounding of what people report. The search leaves them, and until 2026-09-26
they were codes for the hand review (`hora_anterior`, `hora_repetida`, `hora_traslapada`).
TASHA schedules each activity between one trip's arrival and the next start and cannot take an
overlap, and a stay of no minutes is better than one (@sec-revised), so `load_eod` moves such a
start to the minute the previous trip arrives and marks it `hora:llegada`; a start the move of
the trip before pushes into overlap moves with it. The hand passes had done the same, one trip
at a time, for most of them. Since the fourth review of the chains the same move closes a
contradiction of up to `{python} _SLIDE_LIMIT` minutes that the search of @sec-clock found no
reading of the hours for — a 15-minute errand whose return was recorded before it, a drop-off
whose leg minutes overrun the next start — as the first hand pass did ("La salida se recorre…"),
except after a trip to work or school, where a stay of no minutes would make the day implausible
and the review reads the hours instead (@sec-revised).

**Effect.** `{python} fmt(n_slid)` starts in `{python} fmt(slid_people)` people move,
`{python} fmt(slide_short)` of them by the tolerance or less and `{python} slide_cascade` by more,
and the three within-tolerance codes are gone from the rules' output. `{python} slid_at_work` of
the stays of no minutes the moves leave are at work, all within the tolerance: the recorded
times say the person left before arriving, a contradiction of hours the minutes cannot mend.

**The search once more.** The search of @sec-clock reads a chain only if one reading makes all of
it feasible, so a contradiction of minutes that the move to the arrival closes afterwards stood in
the way of reading an hour typed wrong elsewhere in the same chain. Since the fifth review of the
chains (2026-09-26) the chains still infeasible once the starts have moved are searched again, the
moved starts locked, and `{python} counts["chains_read_after_the_slide"]` are read so. Household
834, person 1 (@tbl-ex-again) is one: its escort at 04:30 between work at 08:00 and a return at
18:00 is 16:30, but the visit's return at 20:10 came 28 minutes before the 38-minute ride could
end, which no reading of the hours fixes, so until then the search read nothing; the return moves
to 20:38 and the escort reads as the hand decisions had read it. Run twice over their own output,
the rules now change nothing more.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-again
#| tbl-cap: "A contradiction of minutes that hid an hour typed wrong (household 834, person 1): the return moves to the arrival, then the escort reads as 16:30."
show(person_table(ex_again))
```

## A day read past midnight holds together after it {#sec-night}

A start read as the next day's (@sec-clock) puts the rest of the day on the next calendar day. The
reading stands only where no trip to work or school comes after the trip that passes midnight — a
night shift ends the day, and a day that goes to work again after one is two shifts in one diary —
and where the day's last start then comes less than 24 hours after its first
(`eodgdl.chains._day_wraps`, which the search, the marking and the model's `StartTime` all read).
Until the fifth review of the chains (2026-09-26) the reading stood regardless: 15 days went to work
again after the night, 11 of them running past 24 hours, and the hand review took them for night
shifts because its measure of a day did too. Most are the work, home, work, home diaries whose
first trip to work is recorded in the evening, which the tenth hand round had read one by one:
household 8992, person 1
(@tbl-ex-split) went to work at 21:00 and home at 02:00, to work again at 16:00 and home at 19:00,
a split shift typed on the wrong side of the clock that the eighth hand round had read as 09:00 and
14:00. Held to a day that holds together, the search reads it so, and a day it cannot read keeps
the contradiction as `hora_invertida` for the review (`{python} n_night_voided` trips on the rules'
output). No day `load_eod` returns runs 24 hours.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-split
#| tbl-cap: "Not a night shift (household 8992, person 1): to work at 21:00, home at 02:00, to work again at 16:00. A split shift from 09:00 and 14:00."
show(person_table(ex_split))
```

## Every trip starts where the previous one ended {#sec-origin}

A trip whose origin is not where the previous trip ended breaks the chain. The breaks are
wrong zones, not wrong sequence (@tbl-perm). Sorting the survey's `{python} breaks_raw`
breaks by which side is wrong (@tbl-break-kinds), most follow a *Regresar a Casa* that
reached the household's zone, and in a majority of those the offending origin is a stop
visited at another point of the day, as if carried over from it (@tbl-ex-origin). The
person was at home, so `load_eod` sets that origin to the home zone (`origen:casa`) — the
reading a home-based activity model makes anyway. The other breaks, where a return did not reach
home or an origin is at home after a trip that went elsewhere — most of them a return home that
was never recorded — were left until 2026-09-26, since either side could be wrong. The first hand
pass set the origin of every one of them to the previous trip's destination, and the fourth
review of the chains made that a rule (`origen:anterior`): the row order is the chain, so the
person set out from where the last trip left them (@tbl-ex-continued). This rule and the next
(@sec-copied) invent a value, and `ajustes` says so on every row.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-break-kinds
#| tbl-cap: "The zone-continuity breaks in the shipped table, by which side of the break is wrong. The origin takes the previous destination in every group."
show(break_kinds)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-origin
#| tbl-cap: "A carried-over origin (household 226, person 2): after returning home at 15:15, the 18:05 trip to the clinic starts from the clinic's zone. Its origin becomes home."
show(person_table((226, 2)))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-continued
#| tbl-cap: "A break that does not follow a return home: the trip leaves from where the previous one ended."
show(person_table(ex_continued))
```

**Effect.** `{python} counts["origins_repaired"]` origins go home and `{python} counts["origins_continued"]`
to the previous destination, and the chain breaks fall from `{python} breaks_t2` after the previous
rules to `{python} breaks_clean` in the built table.

## A day's first trip that copies home away starts at home {#sec-copied}

The survey asks once where the day's first trip started and repeats the answer on every row
(@sec-home), and it records that trip's origin zone as well. For `{python} fmt(n_copied)` first
trips the origin is the very AGEB the trip goes to — the destination copied into the origin —
and `{python} fmt(copied_type_too)` copy its place type into the answer too. A trip does not
leave for where it already is: the day started at home, and the fifth hand pass found the trips'
own reported minutes fit a trip from home in 87–92% of them. `load_eod` sets the origin to the
home zone (`origen:copia`) and the person's answer to 'Su casa' (`tipo_origen:copia`, on every
row of the `{python} fmt(n_copied - copied_said_home)` persons who gave another answer;
@tbl-ex-copied). The first hand pass had made this call trip by trip, on every one of them;
since the third review of the chains (2026-09-26) it is a rule.

Two more copies read the same way since the fourth review. `{python} counts["first_origins_answered"]`
first trips leave another zone though the person answered that the day started at home: the
answer, put to the person once and repeated on every row, wins over the one AGEB
(`origen:respuesta`; the first pass moved all of them home). And `{python} counts["first_origins_typed"]`
name their own destination's place type as where the day started — a school
(`{python} int(typed_types.iloc[0])` of them), a factory, a shop — the type copied as the first
reading copied the AGEB (`origen:tipo_copia`, the answer becoming 'Su casa'); the first pass moved
148 of the 160 it reviewed home, and the median distance between the recorded origin and home is
1.4 km. A place where somebody spends the night — another dwelling, a hospital, *Otros* — is
left: the first pass moved 3 of the 20 other dwellings. Neither reading moves a first trip that
goes to the home zone itself, which moved home would go from home to home: it is the rotated
record of @sec-rotated. A first trip that is a return home is left too, and a day that
opens with a return from another AGEB did not start at home whatever the answer says: the
`{python} counts["first_return_answers"]` persons who answered *Su casa* take the place type their
own, their household's or same-occupation trips give that AGEB (`tipo_origen:regreso`), as hand
passes 2 and 3 had done for the same days.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-copied
#| tbl-cap: "A copied origin: the first trip leaves the AGEB it goes to, and the answer to where the day started names the destination's type. The origin becomes home and the answer 'Su casa'."
show(person_table(ex_copied))
```

## A first trip recorded from a place to home went from home to the place {#sec-rotated}

Some days record their first trip turned round: an activity — work, school, a shop — from a place
to the home zone, and the next trip from home onwards. The trip went from home to the place it
names as its origin, and the next left from there. The reading holds where the person answered that
the day started at *Su casa*, or where the next trip is a *Regresar a Casa* from home to home, a
return that makes sense only from the place. `{python} counts["first_trips_rotated"]` first trips
are so recorded; `load_eod` sets their origin home and their destination to the place
(`origen:rotado`, `destino:rotado`), the next trip's origin to the place (`origen:anterior`), the
answer to *Su casa*, and, where the trip was recorded arriving at *Su casa* and the answer names a
place, that place's type (`tipo_destino:rotado`, `{python} n_rotated_typed` trips; @tbl-ex-rotated).
The fifth hand pass had rotated 22 of these days one by one and round 14 of the hand decisions 16
more; 8 had been read by neither, and one the fourth pass read as a return from work. Since the
fifth review of the chains (2026-09-26) it is a rule. A day whose next trip goes somewhere else, or
back to the place, is not rotated: that record says something else — a return from a night shift, a
day that started at the place.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-rotated
#| tbl-cap: "A rotated first trip: recorded from a place to home, then home onwards. It went from home to the place."
show(person_table(ex_rotated))
```

## A return left away from home ends at home, or at a place nothing names {#sec-short}

A *Regresar a Casa* still away from the home zone once its type, a copied destination, the
person's trips and the day-start answer have been read (@sec-mislabel, @sec-copied-return,
@sec-elsewhere) went somewhere nothing names. The day's last trip to an AGEB that no other trip of
the day touches is the return home with the home geocoded in another AGEB, and ends at home
(`destino:casa`, `{python} counts["short_returns_home"]` returns; @tbl-ex-short-home). Any other
went to a place the day leaves from or comes back to, and takes *Otros* as its motive and place type
(`motivo:otros`, `{python} counts["short_returns_other"]`; @tbl-ex-short-other), the O the model
build gave it already. Round 14 of the hand decisions read them so one by one, where the first
hand pass had recoded most of them *Trabajar* or *Estudiar*, for students, children and
homemakers alike; since the fifth review of the chains it is a rule, and `regreso_sin_llegar` is
left only where a hand edit makes one.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-short-home
#| tbl-cap: "A last return to an AGEB nothing else touches: the home, geocoded elsewhere."
show(person_table(ex_short_home))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-short-other
#| tbl-cap: "A return that went to a place the day comes back to or leaves from: 'Otros'."
show(person_table(ex_short_other))
```

## The contract, the validator and the chain report {#sec-contract}

`model_schema.yaml` now defines `TripNumber` as chain order and says explicitly that
`StartTime` need not increase along it; its hours run on past midnight, so a trip on the next
day of a person's diary — from the one marked `hora_nocturna` on — carries 2400 more
(`eodgdl.chains.days_past_midnight`). `validate()` enforces what a builder can
guarantee — trip numbers 1..n, no R/C as an origin, no trip from H to H — and
`tasha.chain_report()` counts what a survey can leave imperfect and a builder cannot repair
without inventing data. On the built tables it reports:

```{python}
#| label: chain-report
#| output: asis
print("```")
for line in chain_lines:
    print(line)
print("```")
```

# What remains {#sec-lingering}

Everything below is counted on the chain `load_eod()` returns once the `{python} n_non_trips`
marked non-trips are set aside (`{python} fmt(len(C))` trips, `{python} fmt(n_days)`
travellers). None of it has a repair that does not invent data, and each defect is a code
in the row's `problemas` column (@tbl-flags), except the early-morning returns of
@tbl-lingering, a suspicion rather than a defect.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-lingering
#| tbl-cap: "Residual defects, as trips and as the person-days they touch, with the `problemas` code that marks each. Weighted share uses the person expansion factor."
ft = flag_tbl.copy()
ft["share of days"] = ft["share of days"].map(pct); ft["weighted share"] = ft["weighted share"].map(pct)
show(ft)
```

## Start times {#sec-lingering-time}

`{python} fmt(int(inv_c.sum()))` trips in `{python} fmt(inv_people)` people still start
before the trip before them: `{python} int(night_c.sum())` look like night or second shifts
(this one by 06:00, the previous trip at or after 18:00, or at or after noon when this one is a
return home; or a return home before 10:00 after a trip to work at or after 18:00, the night
shift of @sec-clock; in a day that holds together after it, @sec-night) and are marked
`hora_nocturna`, and the rest are among the
`{python} fmt(c_beyond.sum())` marked `hora_invertida`: trips that still start before the
previous trip could have arrived by more than the tolerance and are not overnight, chains for
which no reading within the edit menu and the cost cap exists, or several equally cheap ones.
`{python} int(ties_c.sum())` trips share a minute with their predecessor and
`{python} int(left_early_c.sum())` leave an activity before the person could have arrived
there, all of them beyond the tolerance and so `hora_invertida` too: the overlaps within it
moved to the arrival (@sec-arrival), and `hora_anterior`, `hora_repetida` and
`hora_traslapada` are left only where a hand edit makes one. `{python} int(hidden_c.sum())`
in-order returns home between 01:00 and 06:59 may be 12-hour entries the search cannot see,
since they are in order; they carry no code. `{python} n_madrugada` days still start before
05:00 with a trip to anything but work and are marked `hora_madrugada` (@sec-early).

`{python} int(sentinel_c.sum())` trips start at 23:01 as reported and are marked `hora_2301`.
The survey heaps the day's late returns on that minute: `{python} at_23[1]` shipped trips
start at 23:01 against `{python} at_23[2]` at 23:02, `{python} at_23[3]` at 23:03 and
`{python} at_23[4]` at 23:04, `{python} pct(sentinel_last, 0)` of them the person's last trip
and `{python} pct(sentinel_return, 0)` a return home, while the whole hour from 00:00 holds
`{python} hour_0` starts against `{python} fmt(hour_23)` from 23:00 and `{python} hour_1`
from 01:00. The return came at 23:01 or later, likely after midnight; nothing says when, so
the value is kept and marked.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ex-lt1
